active_inquiry.handoff_conclusion: Observed facts: T1 achieved 73% on matched panels with failures concentrated below 14 cm. M3 found 22 non-entries and 5 interrupted holds; interrupted episodes saturated actions, but saturation was also common in successes, branch switching occurred in both successes and failures, and hidden substep excursions were not failure-concentrated. T2 achieved 35%, establishing that the tested fresh full-domain recipe is insufficient without rejecting coverage as a broader method. T3 transferred from T1 with a bounded velocity-aware settling term and achieved 94% on M4 and M5 and 95% on M6, improving near-base performance while preserving strong outer-radius competence. T4 increased the velocity penalty coefficient from 0.25 to 0.5 and fell to 85% on M6, concentrated at 6-10 cm; this rejects that stronger coefficient, not settling control broadly. M7 measured strong compiled saturated responses and approximately 0.07-0.08 rad joint displacement over 20 ms across representative 6-20 cm configurations and both IK branches, without a branch-specific authority collapse. T5 restored the 0.25 coefficient and widened the velocity-aware settling gate from 2 cm to 3 cm. M8 measured T5 at 95% versus T3 at 93% on a fresh shared 100-episode panel; T5 improved 6-10 cm and 14-20 cm strata without regression and retained 100% in 10-14 cm. Interpretation: the T5 result is reproducible evidence that earlier learned braking can improve complete-hold success, so learned approach/transient-braking refinement remains the leading actionable mechanism. The five T5 failures span near-base and outer-radius targets, while M7 and the comparable saturation in M3/M6 do not establish configuration-dependent actuator authority or compiled-dynamics limits as their cause. The residual physical interaction remains unresolved and should be revisited only if further learned refinements fail despite adequate compiled response evidence.
